title: OAuth2 authorisation-code with PKCE against a pluggable external IdP is the project's authentication model
context: A project has one authentication model; the client tier, the server tier, and every operator surface must reason against it. The security-auth-oauth2 blueprint contributes a vendor-neutral shape of that model: identity, sign-in UX, credential storage, MFA, and account recovery live at an external IdP the project selects (Google, GitHub, Microsoft, Okta, Auth0, a corporate ADFS-fronted OIDC, a self-hosted node-oidc-provider); the project owns the flow controller, the provider-adapter seam, the session-bridge, and the sign-in UX composition. A client-tier blueprint (application-spa), a server-tier blueprint (application-api-rest), and every other auth-family blueprint (security-auth-magic-link, security-auth-clerk, security-auth-keycloak when it ships) contribute their own decisions on this topic; blueprint composition surfaces the pairing at add time for the operator to reconcile into one project-level model. That surfacing is intended.
decision: The project's authentication model is delegated identity via OAuth2 authorisation-code flow (RFC 6749 section 4.1) hardened with PKCE (RFC 7636, S256). Identity is proven by a completed round-trip against a project-configured IdP whose declaration satisfies the provider-abstraction contract (REQ-002). The wire credential the browser holds is a project-issued opaque-handle session cookie (`Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`) whose value is neither the provider's access token, the id_token, nor a refresh token; provider tokens are stored server-side on the session record and never round-trip through the browser. For OIDC-declared providers the id_token is verified against the provider's JWKS on every callback (REQ-005). Refresh tokens rotate on every exchange with reuse detection (REQ-007). Sign-out invalidates the project session server-side; provider-side sign-out is an operator-declared option (REQ-008). Multi-provider composition is supported and expressed at the query-parameter layer (REQ-009). Runtime-verify binds the state machine and the identity-lift against a project-authored mock OIDC provider; live-vendor smokes are accountBound (REQ-010).
consequences: The project owns the flow controller, the provider adapter, the session-bridge, and (optionally) the provider selector; the external IdP owns everything else on the identity surface. IdP swap is a provider-record write plus a JWKS-and-endpoint refresh; the flow controller and the session-bridge do not change. Composing with another auth-family blueprint (magic-link, Clerk, Keycloak) conflicts on this topic by design; the expected resolution is one project-level ADR that fixes the identity surface and the credential shape for the whole project. The mock-OIDC-provider runtime-verify posture keeps CI honest without demanding live-vendor credentials in every environment; a project that has live-vendor credentials wires them on top and the accountBound smokes light up. Every path that produces or consumes a session cookie flows through one narrow set of modules the ship gate compels.

alternativesConsidered.name: Passwordless magic-link with server-issued opaque cookie sessions
alternativesConsidered.summary: The security-auth-magic-link blueprint's model: mint a single-use token on POST /login, deliver by email, verify on GET /login/verify, issue an opaque-handle session cookie.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Valid for projects that want no third-party identity dependency and are willing to own the principal registry, the email adapter, the rate-limiter, and the anti-enumeration posture. The trade against OAuth2 is running that whole surface in-house; a project that has a compelling reason to keep identity local (or that has no willing external IdP) takes that trade. This blueprint occupies the other end: identity is delegated, the local surface is small.

alternativesConsidered.name: Hosted identity vendor with vendor-committed shape (Clerk)
alternativesConsidered.summary: The security-auth-clerk blueprint's model: Clerk hosts the sign-in surface, the credential storage, MFA, account recovery; the project runs a middleware boundary against Clerk's session-verification API.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Valid for projects that want the hosted-identity fast lane and are willing to commit to one vendor. The trade against OAuth2-generic is that Clerk (or the equivalent) does more of the work at the cost of a vendor commitment; OAuth2-generic keeps the mechanism vendor-neutral and asks the project to run the flow controller and the session-bridge. Projects that want the hosted lane take the sibling blueprint; projects that need vendor neutrality take this one.

alternativesConsidered.name: Self-hosted OIDC via Keycloak with vendor-committed shape
alternativesConsidered.summary: The forthcoming security-auth-keycloak blueprint's model: run a Keycloak instance, federate through the OIDC authorization-code flow, wire the middleware boundary against Keycloak's realm.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Valid for projects with existing ops capacity and a hard multi-tenant IdP requirement. The trade is running the Keycloak container plus a realm configuration; small rcf-lite projects rarely need it day one. A Keycloak project on this blueprint's contract is one provider record; a Keycloak project on the vendor-committed blueprint is a richer opinion on the realm surface. The choice belongs to the project's ops posture.

alternativesConsidered.name: Direct social sign-in with one hard-coded provider (Google-only, GitHub-only)
alternativesConsidered.summary: Skip the provider abstraction and wire the flow directly against one vendor's URL surface.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Cheap on day one and expensive on day thirty when the project needs a second provider or an operator wants to swap. Every code path branches on the vendor's claim shape and the vendor's cookie names; the abstraction cost is paid over months of rework. This blueprint pays the abstraction cost up front.
